questions.stem: The 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were adopted by the United Nations in the year:
questions.explanation: The SDGs / Agenda 2030 were adopted on 25 September 2015 at a UN summit in New York, to replace the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs, 2000-15). 17 Goals + 169 targets + ~230 indicators, covering poverty, hunger, health, education, gender, water, energy, cities, climate etc. NITI Aayog tracks India's SDG progress through the SDG India Index (first released 2018).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The term 'sustainable development' was made famous in 1987 by a report chaired by:
questions.explanation: The Brundtland Report ('Our Common Future', 1987) by the World Commission on Environment and Development — chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland (former PM of Norway) — defined sustainable development as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. Rachel Carson — 'Silent Spring' (1962), DDT-warning book. Kofi Annan — UN Secretary-General (1997-2006).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The target year for the Sustainable Development Goals is:
questions.explanation: SDGs are also called 'Agenda 2030' because of the 2030 target year. The halfway point (2022-23) saw UN reports warning that progress was off-track on most goals after COVID-19, Ukraine war, inflation. India has committed to LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) as a complementary voluntary framework announced by PM Modi at COP-26 (2021).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Goal 13 of the Sustainable Development Goals focuses on:
questions.explanation: Goal 13 — 'Climate Action' — aims to take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts. Related goals — 7 (affordable clean energy), 6 (water and sanitation), 14 (life below water), 15 (life on land), 11 (sustainable cities), 12 (responsible consumption). Goal 5 is gender equality. Understanding which number maps to which goal is an exam-frequent drill.

options.option_text: Reduce, reuse, recycle — keeping resources in the loop
Replacing all fossil fuels with wind energy
Moving all industrial activity to rural areas

questions.explanation: Circular economy — reduce resource use, reuse products, recycle materials, so outputs become inputs instead of waste. Opposite of the 'linear' take-make-dispose model. Indian policy examples — plastic waste management rules with EPR, battery swapping, e-waste collection, Fly-ash utilisation. Ellen MacArthur Foundation is a leading global champion. The 3 Rs are increasingly supplemented by 'repair' and 'refuse'.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) — a movement championed by India at COP-26 — emphasises:
questions.explanation: Mission LiFE — announced by PM Modi at COP-26 (Glasgow 2021), formally launched 2022 — asks each individual to adopt climate-friendly behaviours (save water, save energy, reduce food waste, avoid single-use plastic, prefer sustainable food, say no to e-waste) rather than expecting change only from governments or industry. The idea is individual agency as a climate lever. UNDP officially backed it in 2022.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) had how many goals?
questions.explanation: MDGs, 2000-15 — eight goals: eradicate extreme poverty/hunger; universal primary education; gender equality; reduce child mortality; maternal health; combat HIV-AIDS, malaria; environmental sustainability; global partnership. Succeeded by the 17 SDGs (2015-30). MDGs were narrower and targeted mainly developing countries; SDGs cover all countries and are broader (cover economic, social, environmental dimensions explicitly).
